tok_001: You can recognise it by the aerial roots hanging off its lower branches like stalactites, the feature that earned it the name Sakasa Icho. It stands in the grounds of Zenpukuji temple in Motoazabu.
tok_002: You can recognise it by the trunk, still hollow and blackened five or six metres up where the firebombs of March 1945 caught it. It stands in the grounds of Sensoji in Asakusa.
tok_003: You can recognise it by the trunk, more than eight metres round and the widest in Ueno Park by a comfortable margin. It stands on the rise by Ueno Toshogu, its canopy shading the approach to the gold-leafed karamon gate.
tok_004: You can recognise it by the trunk, about seven metres round, on the ginkgo that was moved 450 metres across the park in 1902 rather than felled for the road. It stands at the edge of Hibiya Park beside the Matsumotoro restaurant.
tok_005: You can recognise it by Tokyo Tower rising directly behind it: this is the tree in the foreground of everybody's photograph, about 21 metres tall. It stands in front of the gate at Shiba Toshogu.
tok_006: You can recognise it by the low branches, propped on log supports and running more than 20 metres out from the trunk instead of upward. It stands in Hamarikyu Onshi Teien and is the biggest black pine in Tokyo.
tok_007: You can recognise it by the stone marker at its foot, placed in 1956 for the sixtieth anniversary of the discovery made under it. It stands in the Koishikawa Botanical Garden, a female tree that carpets the ground with nuts each autumn.
tok_008: You can recognise it by the trellises of wisteria framing the arched drum bridge, about 50 plants across 15 frames, in flower in late April. It stands in the grounds of Kameido Tenjin.
tok_009: You can recognise it by the 146 ginkgos planted nine metres apart, the tallest 28 metres, all turning gold together in November. It stands as the 300-metre avenue running straight toward the dome of the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery.
tok_010: You can recognise it by the two camphors standing side by side, bound as one by a shimenawa, the sacred straw rope. It stands just in front of the outer worship hall at Meiji Jingu.
tok_011: You can recognise it by the shape, 8.13 metres round against only 10.8 metres tall, a trunk built like a barrel. It stands inside the grounds of Takanawa Community Plaza, a minute from the gates of Shirokanetakanawa Station.
tok_012: You can recognise it by the size, twenty metres tall and four metres round, filling a small triangular junction of low wooden houses. It stands on the open street at the door of the old Mikado bread shop in Yanaka.
tok_013: You can recognise it by the trunk, straight for about seven metres before it opens into an umbrella, seventeen metres tall and four round. It stands beside the Umazaka slope east of Shozenji, a small stone shrine to Akiba at its foot.
tok_016: You can recognise it by the props, eighty-two of them holding up a canopy spreading over 800 square metres from a tree only about eight metres tall. It stands in the grounds of Zenyoji temple in Higashi-Koiwa.
tok_017: You can recognise it by the crowd of trunks pushed out of its own base after lightning split it about six metres up, 10.8 metres round at chest height against 10.2 at the ground. It stands in the grounds of Katsushika Hachimangu.
